newsitem.title: JAPAN: Osaka shareholder group prepares to sue Nomura.
newsitem.headline: Osaka shareholder group prepares to sue Nomura.

text.p: A shareholders' rights group in western Japan said on Thursday it was helping prepare a suit to be filed against the top managers of Nomura Securities over suspected illegal deals.

The lawsuit, to be filed in Tokyo District Court by an unidentified male plaintiff on behalf of all private shareholders, will name Nomura president Hideo Sakamaki and other senior executives, a member of the group said.

Tokuo Sakaguchi, a lawyer and a representative of the Ombudsman Group based in the western Japanese city of Osaka, told Reuters in an interview that it will first urge Nomura next week to sue the two former company directors involved in the case for compensation of some 40 million yen worth of funds they were suspected of funnelling to a corporate client.

If the Nomura executives fail to take action within 30 days of the request, the group will then instruct the plaintiff to file a lawsuit on behalf of shareholders seeking compensation from the executives for losses caused by the scandal.
"We will notify the brokerage in advance that we will also seek additional compensation in case Nomura is forced to suspend business," Sakaguchi said.
Sakaguchi said the loss from any business suspension would be calculated based on an estimate that Nomura earned an average some 1.1 billion yen a day in brokerage commissions last year.
He said the shareholders may seek billions of yen in compensation for such additional losses, depending on the outcome. The group will also seek the resignation of Nomura's top management, he added.
A Nomura spokesman said the company could not comment on the possible suit because such suits are generally settled between the executives of the company concerned and shareholders.

On Monday, two Nomura directors resigned after the brokerage said they made apparently illegal deals and funnelled funds to a corporate client which has been linked by Japanese media to a former "sokaiya" racketeer.

Sokaiya, often linked to "yakuza" crime syndicates, typically try to extort money from firms by threatening to expose dubious business practices or to make a disturbance at yearly shareholders' meetings -- called "sokai" in Japanese.
Companies have also been known to hire sokaiya to muzzle legitimate shareholders' questions at the annual meetings.

Major Japanese asset management firms, including Nomura's own unit Nomura Investment Management Co, and major Japanese trust banks have suspended business with Nomura since the brokerage disclosed the suspected illegal deals.
Most firms said they would wait for the results of a probe by the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC) before resuming business with the scandal-tainted brokerage.
The Finance Ministry said it would decide what steps to take against Nomura after hearing from the SESC, but hinted that the measures might be stern.

The finance minister could, depending on the SESC findings, revoke Nomura's licences or order it to halt some or all business for up to six months. Should the deals be found to have violated the commercial code's ban on payoffs to sokaiya racketeers, legal action could also be initiated.
